job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**S. 2817 drafting review (text as amended October 6, 2026)**

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold:** The 10,000 metric ton trigger applies to "a single vessel," so an operator could split output across several vessels that each stay under the threshold and fall outside the definition.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year":** The bill doesn't say whether this is a calendar year or any rolling 12-month period, or whether it is measured wet or dry.

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "other mineral resources":** Neither term is defined. It is unclear whether "recovery" covers only lifting nodules to the surface or also collection, processing, or discharge, and whether test or pilot collection counts.

4. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's determination:** "The Secretary" is never identified (Commerce, Interior, or another agency), and the bill sets no criteria, notice, hearing, or deadline for the "comparable risk" finding. This is open to an arbitrary-and-capricious or vagueness challenge, which may cut in either direction depending on how the Secretary uses it.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers only individual citizens and corporations organized under state law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies, and "State" is not defined (e.g., whether D.C. or territories are included).

6. **§2(3), "covered vessel":** The 5,000 gross ton threshold for registration doesn't match the 10,000-ton production trigger in §2(1)(A), so a smaller vessel could mine commercially without registering. "Equipped for recovery" is undefined, and the bill doesn't specify which gross tonnage measurement applies.

7. **§3(a), extraterritorial reach:** The prohibition covers "any person in the United States" and "any U.S. person anywhere," which leaves foreign-organized entities and foreign-flagged vessels operating abroad outside its reach. The bill also doesn't address the legal basis for regulating activity in the international seabed Area.

8. **§3(a), "engage in":** This term is undefined and doesn't clearly reach financing, chartering, equipment supply, processing, or importing nodules recovered abroad.

9. **§3(a) and the existing statute:** The bill doesn't amend or reference the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.), which already governs U.S. licensing and permitting for deep seabed activity. The relationship between the two regimes is unclear, and counsel should check for conflict or preemption questions.

10. **§3(b), grandfather clause:** "Exploration license" is undefined and not tied to any statute or agency. The clause also covers "mining conducted under" such a license, which could be read to allow commercial-scale recovery labeled as exploration.

11. **§3(b), scope of grandfather:** The exemption has no volume cap and no expiration, and it is silent on renewals, amendments, expansions, transfers, and commercial recovery permits. Each of these could extend a pre-enactment license indefinitely.

12. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no volume cap, no reporting requirement, no good-faith standard, and no time limit. This is the broadest gap in the bill, since commercial-scale extraction could be recast as assessment.

13. **§4(a), registration:** There is no deadline for initial registration, no required contents, and no definition of "operator." Vessels below the 5,000-ton threshold are not registered at all.

14. **§4(b), quarterly reports:** The reports must only "describe" recovery activities, with no minimum data (tonnage, location, depth, sampling), no verification or audit, and no public availability. Self-certification plus possible trade-secret claims could make the reports largely uninformative.

15. **§5, penalty scope:** Civil and criminal penalties attach only to violations of §3, so failing to register or report under §4 carries no penalty. This is a significant enforcement gap.

16. **§5(a) and §8, effective date conflict:** §5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays effectiveness by 180 days. This creates ambiguity about whether conduct in the gap is penalized and invites a rush to ramp up operations before the prohibition takes effect.

17. **§5(a), enforcement mechanics:** The bill does not designate an enforcing agency, define a "day" for continuing violations, provide for injunctive relief, authorize vessel or equipment forfeiture, or create a citizen suit provision. The result is weak enforcement tools and room for litigation over procedure.

18. **§5(b), criminal liability:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill has no responsible-officer, aiding-and-abetting, or financing liability for individuals. The limitations period is also unspecified, so it defaults to five years under 18 U.S.C. §3282.

19. **§6, international agreement:** The Secretary of State need only "seek to negotiate," with no obligation to conclude an agreement, no reporting requirement, no definition of "equivalent," and no mechanism tying the agreement to suspension of the prohibition.

20. **§7(a), joint resolution standard:** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say whether the National Academies report is a precondition to congressional action or what deadline applies. A joint resolution would also be subject to presidential veto, requiring a two-thirds override if the President objects.

21. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), duration conflict:** §7(a) makes the prohibition indefinite, but §7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years, which makes §7(a) largely moot. The sunset also has no savings clause, so it is unclear whether violations or pending enforcement actions survive expiration.

22. **No severability clause:** If a court strikes §2(1)(B) or §7(a) as unconstitutionally vague or as an improper delegation, the whole Act could fall with it. Opponents will likely press these challenges, so the Act's vulnerability here is a key point for the markup.

23. **No definition of "person" (low priority):** 1 U.S.C. §1 supplies a default definition that likely covers corporations, so this is more a clarity issue than a real gap.

**Priorities for the markup:** Items 12 (§3(c)), 10–11 (§3(b)), 15 (§5 penalty scope), 1 (per-vessel threshold), and 21 (§7 duration conflict) are the most consequential, since each affects whether the prohibition has real effect.

**Caveats:** Several items are double-edged. Vague terms such as "comparable" in §2(1)(B) and "serious harm" in §7(a) create litigation risk for the bill's proponents, but they also give the Secretary broad discretion to read the bill against us. Before relying on these points in advocacy, have counsel confirm the interaction with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act and check the current committee text, since this analysis is based only on the text you provided.
